```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
# The estimator of the case study, for spec_frame() and the conversion rule of the robustness study
source("../R/_tools.R")

housing <- readr::read_csv("../data/housing_emails.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
analysts <- readr::read_csv("../data/analysts5.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
marks <- readr::read_csv("../data/reference_marks.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
curve <- readr::read_csv("../data/spec_curve.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
# The counts of the four groups of replies, recovered from display_replication.csv
# by companion/_model-outputs/bayes_housing.R
counts <- readr::read_csv("_model-outputs/bayes_housing_counts.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
ref <- datawizard::data_filter(curve, is_reference)
oa <- datawizard::data_filter(marks, id == "OA")
replication <- readr::read_csv("../data/display_replication.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
subcounty <- datawizard::data_filter(replication, population == "replies", authorities == "sub-county")
```

Placing results on one scale and combining them is the subject of this module of the [companion curriculum](index.qmd), which works through the two kinds of comparison raised by the Housing and racial bias case study. The case study rests on a field experiment, presented in full on the [background page](../background.qmd), in which the original authors emailed public housing authorities in the United States from names meant to indicate a white, a Black or a Hispanic applicant. The authors found that replies to the Hispanic names opened with the sender's name less often [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect]. Five analysts reanalysed the claim in the SCORE robustness study [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness], each working on the original authors' public file, while a new experiment conducted for the SCORE replicability study attempted to replicate the claim on new data. The first comparison sets five analyses of one file side by side, and the second two studies of the same question. Meta-analysis offers tools for the second comparison, whereas the first, as the module argues, needs a different kind of summary. Every number on the page is computed from the case-study files in `data/` when the page is built.

## 1. What a meta-analysis combines {#sec-what}

A meta-analysis combines the estimates of one quantity from several studies into a summary in which each estimate is weighted by its precision, a study with a small standard error thus counting for more than a noisy one. The weights are the inverse of the sampling variance of each estimate, and the pooled estimate has a smaller standard error than any of the studies on which it rests, because the studies are taken to be independent draws of evidence about the quantity. Two models are in common use, the first of which, the equal-effects model, assumes that every study estimates the same true effect and that the estimates differ only by sampling error. A random-effects model, by contrast, lets the true effects differ from study to study around an average, and estimates the variance of that distribution, usually written $\tau^2$, beside its mean. Both models are fitted by the metafor package, together with Cochran's Q-test of whether the studies differ more than sampling error would lead one to expect [@Viechtbauer2010ConductingMetaanalysesMetafor]. The author of the package also points to a third reading, the fixed-effects model, which computes the same weighted average as the equal-effects model but claims less for it. The fixed-effects model "provides an answer to the question: How large is the average true effect in the set of k studies included in the meta-analysis?", and it therefore, "contrary to what is often stated in the literature", does not assume that the true effects are the same [@Viechtbauer2010ConductingMetaanalysesMetafor, p. 4].

What the choice between the models commits one to is explained in *Bayesian Data Analysis*, where meta-analysis is said to rest on "the overarching assumption that the studies are comparable in some broad sense". Within that assumption three possibilities arise: the studies may be "identical replications of each other", may be "so different that the results of any one study provide no information about the results of any of the others", or may be exchangeable, different from each other but in ways that are "not expected a priori to have predictable effects favoring one study over another" [@GelmanEtAl2014BayesianDataAnalysis, pp. 125–126]. The first possibility corresponds to the equal-effects model and the third to the random-effects model, each answering a different question, and once the studies are few, the question arguably matters more than the arithmetic.

## 2. The common scale of the robustness study {#sec-scale}

The robustness study approached the problem from the other side, its analysts reporting a test statistic of their own choosing for Task 2, from the families of "r, z-test, t-test, F-test or χ2 test", together with their sample sizes and degrees of freedom, a procedure through which "most results could be translated into standardized coefficients by the coordinators" [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness, Methods]. The article describes the conversion as "a practical solution", adding that "these transformations have limitations and their calculation relies on assumptions that may not hold in all considered analysis settings" [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness, p. 136]. The conversion rules are contained in the script `standard_correlation_coefficient.R`, published by the robustness-study team (github.com/marton-balazs-kovacs/multi100), and are quoted here as they appear there:

```r
# z: the sample size stands in for the degrees of freedom
tanh(abs(test_statistic)*sqrt(1/(sample_size-3)))*sign(test_statistic)
# chi2: read as the square of a z
tanh(sqrt(abs(test_statistic))*sqrt(1/(sample_size-3)))*sign(test_statistic)
# t: with its degrees of freedom
sqrt(abs(test_statistic)^2/(test_statistic^2+df1))*sign(test_statistic)
```

Each correlation was then converted into a Cohen's d by the rule contained in the script `cohens_d.R` from the same team, `sign(r)*sqrt(4/((1/r^2)-1))`, which corresponds to $d = 2r/\sqrt{1 - r^2}$. The course estimator implements the first three rules in `r_robustness()` in `R/_tools.R`, and when applied to the four statistics recorded in the robustness study for this claim, it returns the four recorded correlations.

```{r}
#| label: conversion
# The d rule is quoted from cohens_d.R of the team of the robustness study; the
# recorded d is positive for all four, because the team took the direction from
# the box that each analyst ticked
recorded <- analysts |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(statistic_recorded)) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(
    r_rule = r_robustness(statistic_recorded, statistic_type, NA, n_recorded),
    d_rule = sign(r_rule) * sqrt(4 / ((1 / r_rule^2) - 1))
  ) |>
  datawizard::data_select(c("id", "statistic_type", "statistic_recorded", "n_recorded",
                            "r_recorded", "r_rule", "d_recorded", "d_rule"))
recorded |> dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(dplyr::where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

The rule reproduces every recorded correlation, sign included, and every d up to its sign, a sign set separately by the robustness study, in which the effect sizes of the reanalyses "are negative only when they indicate an opposite effect compared with the original study" [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness, Methods]. The project then asked how often a reanalysis lay "within the tolerance region of ±0.05 Cohen's d" of the original result, a criterion met by 34% of the 396 available effect sizes [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness, p. 136].

## 3. The five housing analysts on that scale {#sec-five}

@tbl-five presents the five analyses of the claim both on the scale of the robustness study and on the scale of the claim itself, the gap in the share of replies that opened with the sender's name, in percentage points.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-five
#| tbl-cap: "The five analyses of the Housing claim in the robustness study: the recorded statistic, the emails on which it was converted, the recorded correlation and Cohen's d, and the gap between Hispanic and comparison names in the course refit of each analysis. Source: `data/analysts5.csv`."
#| echo: false
# dplyr, because datawizard reads the column name `d` on the left as a reference
analysts |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    Statistic = dplyr::case_when(is.na(statistic_recorded) ~ "none recorded",
                                 statistic_type == "chi2" ~ paste0("χ<sup>2</sup> = ", sprintf("%.3f", statistic_recorded)),
                                 .default = paste("z =", sub("^-", "−", sprintf("%.3f", statistic_recorded)))),
    Emails = dplyr::if_else(is.na(n_recorded), "–", as.character(n_recorded)),
    r = dplyr::if_else(is.na(r_recorded), "–", sub("^-", "−", sprintf("%.3f", r_recorded))),
    d = dplyr::if_else(is.na(d_recorded), "–", sprintf("%.3f", d_recorded)),
    `Gap (points)` = sub("^-", "−", sprintf("%.1f", b_pp_refit))
  ) |>
  datawizard::data_select(c(Analyst = "id", Comparison = "comparison", "Statistic", "Emails", "r", "d",
                            "Gap (points)")) |>
  tinytable::tt() |>
  tinytable::style_tt(j = 4:7, align = "r")
```

All five analysts found Hispanic names greeted by name less often, by `r insight::format_value(abs(max(analysts$b_pp_refit)), digits = 1)` to `r insight::format_value(abs(min(analysts$b_pp_refit)), digits = 1)` points, yet the column of correlations runs from `r insight::format_value(min(analysts$r_recorded, na.rm = TRUE), digits = 3, style_negative = "minus")` to `r insight::format_value(max(analysts$r_recorded, na.rm = TRUE), digits = 3)`, with one row left empty. That column is the product of five features of this case study, each of which can be checked on the data.

**An analyst without a recorded statistic.** P9W8Y has no row in the conversion above, because the robustness study recorded no statistic for this analysis, although the analyst's report gives $\chi^2$(2, N = 558) = 15.951 for the omnibus test of the three groups, matching the value of the course refit. The analysis is therefore absent from every summary of the project that works on d, and it is also the analysis whose Task 1 verdict was "no evidence either way".

**A test of three groups.** The statistic reported by P9W8Y tests whether the three groups of names differ at all, on two degrees of freedom, whereas the rule for a $\chi^2$ reads a statistic as the square of a single z, a reading that holds only on one degree of freedom. Applied regardless, the rule would yield a correlation, but that number would describe how far the three groups differ from one another, rather than the gap between Hispanic and white names stated in the claim.

```{r}
#| label: three-groups
p9w8y <- datawizard::data_filter(analysts, id == "P9W8Y")
round(r_robustness(p9w8y$statistic_refit, "chi2", NA, p9w8y$n_refit), 3)
```

**A $\chi^2$ carries no sign.** As a sum of squares, a $\chi^2$ is positive whichever group was greeted by name more often, which is why the correlations recorded for 8PTRZ and 25N5D are positive although both gaps are negative. The correlations recorded for UYV3F and EWFMI, by contrast, take the sign of a z, which depends on the feature described next.

**The base group sets the sign of a z.** UYV3F fitted a logistic regression of the greeting on an indicator of the Hispanic names, with white names as the base, while EWFMI made the same comparison in a model with the Hispanic names as the base. Since the two models describe one gap in opposite directions, the z statistics of the two models, and the correlations computed from these statistics, carry opposite signs, as the chunk below shows by reversing the base in the model used by UYV3F.

```{r}
#| label: base-group
frame_white <- spec_frame(housing, comparison = "white", population = "replies", uncoded = "drop") |>
  datawizard::data_modify(white = 1 - hisp)
z_white_base <- glm(y ~ hisp, family = binomial(), data = frame_white) |>
  parameters::model_parameters() |>
  datawizard::data_filter(Parameter == "hisp")
z_hisp_base <- glm(y ~ white, family = binomial(), data = frame_white) |>
  parameters::model_parameters() |>
  datawizard::data_filter(Parameter == "white")
round(c(white_base = z_white_base$z, hispanic_base = z_hisp_base$z), 3)
round(r_robustness(c(z_white_base$z, z_hisp_base$z), "z", NA, nrow(frame_white)), 3)
```

**The continuity correction moves a recorded value.** `chisq.test()` and `prop.test()` in R apply Yates's continuity correction to a two-by-two table unless instructed otherwise, and the two analysts who recorded a $\chi^2$ kept this default, as shown in the [binary-outcomes module](binary-outcomes.qmd#sec-difference).

```{r}
#| label: continuity
frame_8ptrz <- spec_frame(housing, comparison = "nonhispanic", population = "replies", uncoded = "drop")
frame_25n5d <- spec_frame(housing, comparison = "white", population = "all", uncoded = "not_named")
tab_8ptrz <- table(frame_8ptrz$hisp, frame_8ptrz$y)
tab_25n5d <- table(frame_25n5d$hisp, frame_25n5d$y)[, 2:1]
chi <- c(`8PTRZ corrected` = unname(chisq.test(tab_8ptrz)$statistic),
         `8PTRZ uncorrected` = unname(chisq.test(tab_8ptrz, correct = FALSE)$statistic),
         `25N5D corrected` = unname(prop.test(tab_25n5d)$statistic),
         `25N5D uncorrected` = unname(prop.test(tab_25n5d, correct = FALSE)$statistic))
round(chi, 3)
round(r_robustness(chi, "chi2", NA, c(nrow(frame_8ptrz), nrow(frame_8ptrz), nrow(frame_25n5d), nrow(frame_25n5d))), 4)
```

Without the correction, 8PTRZ would have recorded $\chi^2$ = `r insight::format_value(chi[["8PTRZ uncorrected"]], digits = 3)` rather than `r insight::format_value(chi[["8PTRZ corrected"]], digits = 3)`, and 25N5D `r insight::format_value(chi[["25N5D uncorrected"]], digits = 3)` rather than `r insight::format_value(chi[["25N5D corrected"]], digits = 3)`, and although the resulting correlations move only in the third decimal, the move stems from a default setting of the software, not from the data or the question.

How these features combine is apparent from the tolerance region used in the robustness study. The robustness study recorded the original result as z = `r insight::format_value(abs(oa$statistic), digits = 2)` on `r oa$n` replies, the coefficient of the Hispanic names divided by its standard error (−0.82 and 0.22) in the logistic regression fitted by the original authors with covariates and all three groups (Table 1, p. 37), a z that converts to r = `r insight::format_value(r_robustness(abs(oa$statistic), "z", NA, oa$n), digits = 3)` and d = `r insight::format_value(2 * r_robustness(abs(oa$statistic), "z", NA, oa$n) / sqrt(1 - r_robustness(abs(oa$statistic), "z", NA, oa$n)^2), digits = 3)`.

```{r}
#| label: tolerance
r_oa <- r_robustness(abs(oa$statistic), "z", NA, oa$n)
d_oa <- 2 * r_oa / sqrt(1 - r_oa^2)
recorded |>
  datawizard::data_modify(gap_pp = analysts$b_pp_refit[match(id, analysts$id)],
                          distance_d = d_recorded - d_oa,
                          within_tolerance = abs(distance_d) <= 0.05) |>
  datawizard::data_select(c("id", "gap_pp", "d_recorded", "distance_d", "within_tolerance")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(dplyr::where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

Three of the four recorded analyses fall within ±0.05 of the original d, the one outside being UYV3F, whose gap of `r insight::format_value(analysts$b_pp_refit[analysts$id == "UYV3F"], digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` points is exactly the raw gap reported in the paper. The z recorded for UYV3F comes from a model without covariates on `r analysts$n_refit[analysts$id == "UYV3F"]` replies, against a model with covariates on `r oa$n`, and the conversion turns that difference in model and sample into a difference in d of `r insight::format_value(analysts$d_recorded[analysts$id == "UYV3F"] - d_oa, digits = 3)`. The analysis by 25N5D, meanwhile, lands within the region, although its gap among all delivered emails is about seven points smaller than the published one. On this claim the common scale appears to rank the analyses partly by their test statistics and sample sizes, which is the limitation flagged by the article itself. The course instead places every analysis on the scale of the claim, in percentage points, as explained on the [background page](../background.qmd#sec-scale).

## 4. Five analyses of one file {#sec-one-file}

The five analyses are not five studies, since the analyses share every email, every reply and every greeting code. Any sampling error contained in the file is therefore carried by all five at once, and if the authorities had answered a little differently in 2014, all five estimates would have moved together. What separates the five analyses are the decisions made by each analyst about which names to compare, which emails to count, which model to fit and which statistic to report. The spread of the five results therefore measures the effect of analytical choices on one sample, which is what the robustness study set out to measure, while indicating nothing about sampling error. The same applies to the specification curve of the case study, all `r nrow(curve)` specifications of which are fitted to the same file.

A pooled estimate of such results arguably answers no clear question. The inverse-variance weights treat each result as an independent piece of evidence, and the standard error of the pool shrinks as the number of results grows. The metafor package will fit the model without complaint, as the chunk below shows for the specification curve.

```{r}
#| label: pool-curve
pooled_curve <- metafor::rma(yi = b_pp, sei = se_pp, method = "EE", data = curve)
round(c(estimate = pooled_curve$beta[[1]], se = pooled_curve$se, se_one_spec = stats::median(curve$se_pp)), 2)
```

The pooled gap has a standard error of `r insight::format_value(pooled_curve$se, digits = 2)` points, as if `r nrow(curve)` independent experiments of `r min(curve$n)` to `r max(curve$n)` emails had been run, when in fact there was a single experiment, whose reference comparison has a standard error of `r insight::format_value(ref$se_pp, digits = 2)` points. Since the estimate is an average over a menu of specifications whose make-up was chosen by the course, even its centre depends on how many options each decision was given, while its standard error belongs to no sampling process.

Analyses of one file can be summarised by their spread and by what drives it. On this claim, all five analyses and all `r nrow(curve)` specifications yield a gap in the direction of the claim, and each of the five tests reported by the analysts for Task 2 is significant at the 5% level. The gaps found by the five analysts range from `r insight::format_value(min(analysts$b_pp_refit), digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` to `r insight::format_value(max(analysts$b_pp_refit), digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` points and those on the specification curve from `r insight::format_value(min(curve$b_pp), digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` to `r insight::format_value(max(curve$b_pp), digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")`, with a standard deviation of `r insight::format_value(stats::sd(curve$b_pp), digits = 1)` points across the specifications, smaller than the standard error of any single specification. The range, the share of results in each direction and the share that are significant describe the robustness of the claim to analytical choices, while the decomposition of the curve by its decisions, presented in the [multiverse module](multiverse.qmd), indicates which choices produce the spread. Two verdicts of "no evidence either way" are recorded beside these numbers, both of which are traced on the [background page](../background.qmd#sec-verdicts) to the questions asked by the two analysts rather than to their estimates. A spread of this kind is the counterpart of what @GelmanLoken2014StatisticalCrisisScience call the 'garden of forking paths', the many analyses that the same data allow, each of which a researcher could have chosen in the light of the data. On this claim the analyses chosen by the five analysts and by the course all yield a gap in the same direction.

## 5. Two studies of one question {#sec-two-studies}

The original experiment and the replication are a different matter. The replication emailed a wider set of authorities, 3,050 against 1,017, in 2020 rather than 2014 and from new names, and since its sampling error is independent of that of the original, the two estimates constitute two pieces of evidence about the gap, to which meta-analysis applies. The comparison below uses the reference specification of the course, Hispanic against white names among the coded replies with no covariates, together with the same comparison among all replies to the replication, the comparison by which the replication is marked on the specification curve. Its counts are taken from the shares and the total given in `display_replication.csv`, recovered by the script `companion/_model-outputs/bayes_housing.R`.

```{r}
#| label: escalc
two <- tibble::tibble(
  study = c("Original experiment, 2014", "Replication, 2020"),
  k_hisp = counts$k[counts$hisp == 1], n_hisp = counts$n[counts$hisp == 1],
  k_white = counts$k[counts$hisp == 0], n_white = counts$n[counts$hisp == 0]
)
# The risk difference, the scale of the claim, in percentage points
gaps <- metafor::escalc(measure = "RD", ai = k_hisp, n1i = n_hisp, ci = k_white, n2i = n_white,
                        data = two) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(yi = 100 * yi, vi = 100^2 * vi)
equal <- metafor::rma(yi, vi, method = "EE", data = gaps)
random <- metafor::rma(yi, vi, method = "REML", data = gaps)
summary(gaps) |> datawizard::data_select(c("study", "yi", "sei", "ci.lb", "ci.ub"))
equal
```

```{r}
#| label: tau
random
stats::confint(random)
```

The equal-effects model pools the two gaps to `r insight::format_value(equal$beta[[1]], digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` points (95% CI `r insight::format_value(equal$ci.lb, digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` to `r insight::format_value(equal$ci.ub, digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")`), much closer to the replication than to the original, because the replication has about four times as many replies and thus about four times the weight. The test of heterogeneity rejects the equal-effects assumption, Q = `r insight::format_value(equal$QE, digits = 2)` on 1 degree of freedom (`r insight::format_p(equal$QEp, stars = FALSE)`), indicating that the two gaps differ by more than sampling error leads one to expect. The random-effects model estimates the standard deviation of the true gaps at $\tau$ = `r insight::format_value(sqrt(random$tau2), digits = 1)` points, with a confidence interval from `r insight::format_value(stats::confint(random)$random["tau", "ci.lb"], digits = 1)` to `r insight::format_value(stats::confint(random)$random["tau", "ci.ub"], digits = 1)` points, and its pooled gap of `r insight::format_value(random$beta[[1]], digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` points comes with an interval from `r insight::format_value(random$ci.lb, digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` to +`r insight::format_value(random$ci.ub, digits = 1)`, wide enough to contain the estimates of both studies as well as gaps in either direction. @fig-forest presents the four results, the two studies and the two pooled estimates.

```{r}
#| label: fig-forest
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 2.8
#| fig-cap: "The gap in greetings by name between Hispanic and white names among the coded replies, in the original experiment and in the replication, with 95% confidence intervals, and the two pooled estimates. The size of each square is proportional to the weight of the study in the equal-effects model. Sources: `data/housing_emails.csv`, `data/display_replication.csv`."
#| fig-alt: "Forest plot. The original experiment lies at about −20 points with an interval from about −30 to −10; the replication lies at about 0 with an interval from about −5 to +5; the equal-effects pool lies near −4 with a narrow interval, and the random-effects pool near −10 with an interval from about −29 to +9."
forest <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  summary(gaps) |>
    tibble::as_tibble() |>
    dplyr::transmute(label = study, estimate = yi, low = ci.lb, high = ci.ub,
                     weight = stats::weights(equal), kind = "study"),
  tibble::tibble(label = c("Pooled, equal effects", "Pooled, random effects"),
                 estimate = c(equal$beta[[1]], random$beta[[1]]),
                 low = c(equal$ci.lb, random$ci.lb), high = c(equal$ci.ub, random$ci.ub),
                 weight = NA_real_, kind = "pooled")
) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(label = factor(label, levels = rev(label)))
ggplot2::ggplot(forest, ggplot2::aes(x = estimate, y = label)) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "#9aa8b3") +
  ggplot2::geom_errorbar(ggplot2::aes(xmin = low, xmax = high), width = 0.15, colour = "#1d2733") +
  ggplot2::geom_point(data = \(d) datawizard::data_filter(d, kind == "study"),
                      ggplot2::aes(size = weight), shape = 15, colour = "#0e3b6a") +
  ggplot2::geom_point(data = \(d) datawizard::data_filter(d, kind == "pooled"),
                      shape = 18, size = 4.5, colour = "#8b1538") +
  ggplot2::scale_size_area(max_size = 6, guide = "none") +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(labels = \(x) sub("^-", "−", x)) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "gap in greetings by name, Hispanic minus white names (points)", y = NULL) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  ggplot2::theme(panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank())
```

Neither pooled estimate appears to carry much weight. The equal-effects pool assumes the first of the three possibilities described in *Bayesian Data Analysis*, that the two experiments are identical replications, an assumption rejected by the data. Read as a fixed-effects model, the same number is the weighted average of the true gaps in these two experiments, a valid summary of the two studies but of nothing beyond them. The random-effects pool assumes the third possibility, that the two experiments are exchangeable draws from a population of possible experiments, and estimates the spread of that population from two of its members, which is why the interval for $\tau$ runs from a few points to more than forty. With only two studies, the average of this population is barely estimable, and its spread not at all. A reader who wishes to know how often public housing officials greet a Hispanic applicant by name less often than a white one is likely to learn more from the two estimates and the differences between the two designs than from either pool. The two studies used different names, emailed a different set of authorities and were conducted six years apart, while the pooled number averages over all of these differences without identifying any of them.

## 6. Equivalence and difference {#sec-equivalence}

The replication found no significant gap, but a non-significant result does not show that the gap is zero or small, a question asked directly by an equivalence test. @LakensEtAl2020ImprovingInferencesNull describe the logic: "To perform an equivalence test, researchers first have to determine a 'smallest effect size of interest,' the smallest effect they deem meaningful", then test against a lower and an upper bound set at that size, and if both one-sided tests reject, "we can reject the hypothesis that the true effect is as extreme as or more extreme than our smallest effect size of interest" (p. 47). Known as the two one-sided tests, or TOST, the procedure amounts to asking whether the 90% confidence interval of the estimate lies within the bounds.

The smallest effect size of interest has to be argued for, and the case study offers one argument that does not depend on taste. Where the original study states no such size, "one way to decide upon a smallest effect size of interest is to assume that the authors were only interested in effects that could have yielded a significant result, and then look at the effect sizes that could have been statistically significant given the sample size they collected" [@LakensEtAl2020ImprovingInferencesNull, p. 50]. Since the reference comparison of the original experiment has a standard error of `r insight::format_value(ref$se_pp, digits = 2)` points on `r ref$df` degrees of freedom, a gap had to exceed about `r insight::format_value(ref$se_pp * stats::qt(0.975, ref$df), digits = 1)` points before the original study could report it as significant. As a gap smaller than that could not have produced the published finding, a replication that rules out gaps of that size has shown that the effect, if there is one, is too small for the original design to have detected. Two stricter bounds, one of 5 points (a difference of one reply in twenty) and one of 3 points, show how far the conclusion depends on the bound chosen.

```{r}
#| label: tost
critical_gap <- ref$se_pp * stats::qt(0.975, ref$df)
bounds <- c(critical_gap, 5, 3)
repl <- datawizard::data_filter(two, study == "Replication, 2020")
orig <- datawizard::data_filter(two, study == "Original experiment, 2014")
tost <- purrr::map(list(replication = repl, original = orig), \(s) {
  purrr::map(bounds, \(b) {
    test <- TOSTER::twoprop_test(p1 = s$k_hisp / s$n_hisp, p2 = s$k_white / s$n_white,
                                 n1 = s$n_hisp, n2 = s$n_white, null = b / 100,
                                 alternative = "equivalence")
    tibble::tibble(bound = b, low_90 = 100 * test$conf.int[1], high_90 = 100 * test$conf.int[2],
                   p_tost = test$p.value)
  }) |>
    purrr::list_rbind()
}) |>
  purrr::list_rbind(names_to = "study")
tost |> dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(c("bound", "low_90", "high_90"), \(x) round(x, 1)),
                                p_tost = signif(p_tost, 3))
```

```{r}
#| label: tost-values
#| include: false
tost_repl <- datawizard::data_filter(tost, study == "replication")
```

Since the 90% interval of the replication runs from `r insight::format_value(tost_repl$low_90[1], digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` to `r insight::format_value(tost_repl$high_90[1], digits = 1)` points, the two one-sided tests reject gaps as large as the critical gap of the original study (`r insight::format_p(tost_repl$p_tost[1], stars = FALSE)`) and as large as 5 points (`r insight::format_p(tost_repl$p_tost[2], stars = FALSE)`), but not gaps as large as 3 points (`r insight::format_p(tost_repl$p_tost[3], stars = FALSE)`). The replication is therefore statistically equivalent to no gap within the resolution of the original study, and within 5 points, although a gap of a few points in either direction remains compatible with its results. The original experiment, by contrast, is equivalent to no gap under none of the bounds, since its interval lies far below all three.

That the replication is equivalent to zero while the original found a significant gap does not, by itself, show that the two studies disagree. @GelmanStern2006DifferenceSignificantNot made the point in the title of their article, "The Difference Between 'Significant' and 'Not Significant' is not Itself Statistically Significant", and a comparison of two studies requires a test of the difference between them, which a meta-regression with the study as its moderator provides.

```{r}
#| label: moderator
difference <- metafor::rma(yi, vi, mods = ~ study, method = "EE", data = gaps)
difference
```

The replication gap exceeds the original gap by `r insight::format_value(difference$beta[[2]], digits = 1)` points (95% CI `r insight::format_value(difference$ci.lb[2], digits = 1)` to `r insight::format_value(difference$ci.ub[2], digits = 1)`), and the test of the moderator, `r insight::format_p(difference$QMp, stars = FALSE)`, is the test of heterogeneity from section 5 under another name, as it must be with two studies. Here the two studies do differ, beyond what sampling error explains, although the test cannot establish why. The names, the authorities, the year and the selection of a striking original result by its significance are all candidates, and the [Bayesian estimation module](bayesian.qmd#sec-design) asks how much of the original gap the last of these candidates could explain. On the log-odds scale, which `escalc(measure = "OR")` computes from the same counts, the conclusions remain the same.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Rerun the chunk `escalc` with `measure = "OR"` and compare the test of heterogeneity with the one on the scale of percentage points. Then replace the replication counts with those among the sub-county authorities, which the replication kept to match the paper: `display_replication.csv` gives their shares and their total of `r format(subcounty$n, big.mark = ",")` replies, and the split of those replies into groups has to be recovered as the script `bayes_housing.R` does for all replies. Finally, choose a smallest effect size of interest of your own for the TOST, write two sentences that justify it from the case study, and check whether the conclusion changes.
:::

## 7. The robustness study as a whole {#sec-robustness}

The problems examined on this page concern one claim and its five analysts, whereas the project as a whole is taken up in the [discussion of the robustness article](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/robustness-article.html) on the AR4DS site. That discussion covers the design of the project across 100 studies and 504 reanalyses, the conversion to a common scale with its tolerance regions, and what the project concluded about the robustness of the social and behavioural sciences to analytical choices.

## Sources and further reading {#sec-sources}

The models on this page are fitted with metafor, and the article describing the package [@Viechtbauer2010ConductingMetaanalysesMetafor] offers a full introduction to it, from the computation of effect sizes with `escalc()` to meta-regression. The three possibilities open to a meta-analysis, and the estimands implied by each, are described in *Bayesian Data Analysis* [@GelmanEtAl2014BayesianDataAnalysis, section 5.6], while equivalence tests and their bounds are treated in @LakensEtAl2020ImprovingInferencesNull, beside Bayes factors for the same question. The conversion rules and the tolerance region are those given in the article on the robustness study and in its code [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness]. The numbers rest on the files `analysts5.csv`, `reference_marks.csv`, `spec_curve.csv`, `housing_emails.csv` and `display_replication.csv` in `data/`, each with a codebook, and on the replication counts stored in `companion/_model-outputs/bayes_housing_counts.csv`.
